subject: science
title: US Middle School Science - Earth Structure and Rocks Reading
subtitle: Reading passages on Earth's layers, mineral evidence, rock formation, data interpretation, and human uses of rocks.
description: A reading pack for practising evidence-based explanations about Earth's interior, minerals, rocks, and the rock cycle. Passages use source-grounded examples and questions that mix fact retrieval, inference, and scientific reasoning.

data.sourcePassage: Earth is made of layers with different materials and properties. The crust is the thin, solid rocky layer at the surface. Below it, the mantle is much thicker and is made of hot, mostly solid rock that can flow slowly over long periods of time. Beneath the mantle is the outer core, a liquid layer made mostly of iron and nickel. At the center is the inner core, a solid metal sphere. Earth's layers formed partly because denser materials sank toward the center when early Earth was forming. Less dense rocky materials stayed closer to the surface. The layers interact with other Earth systems. Heat from inside Earth helps move mantle material, and this movement is connected to plate motion, volcanoes, earthquakes, and mountain building.

questions.question: Which Earth layer is the thin, solid rocky layer at the surface?
questions.modelAnswer: The crust is the thin, solid rocky layer at the surface.

questions.question: Which layer is liquid and made mostly of iron and nickel?
questions.modelAnswer: Outer core

questions.question: Why did dense materials move toward Earth's center as early Earth formed?
questions.modelAnswer: Denser materials such as iron and nickel sank toward the center, while less dense rocky materials stayed nearer the surface.

questions.question: How is heat inside Earth connected to surface changes?
questions.modelAnswer: Internal heat helps move mantle material, which is connected to plate motion, volcanoes, earthquakes, and mountain building.

questions.question: What makes Earth a system rather than just separate layers?
questions.modelAnswer: Earth is a system because its layers and other parts interact; energy and matter move between them and cause changes over time.

data.sourcePassage: Scientists cannot travel to Earth's center, and the deepest human-made holes reach only a tiny distance into the crust. To study the inside of Earth, scientists use indirect evidence. Seismic waves from earthquakes are especially useful because they travel through Earth and change behavior when they pass through different materials. Some waves bend as they move through layers with different properties. Some waves do not pass through liquid layers. When seismometers around the world record wave arrivals after an earthquake, scientists compare the patterns with models of Earth's interior. Missing wave patterns can support the claim that part of Earth's interior is liquid, such as the outer core. Seismic evidence works best when combined with other evidence, including density calculations, volcanic rocks, magnetic field data, meteorites, and laboratory experiments.

questions.question: Why are seismic waves useful for studying Earth's interior?
options: They change behavior as they travel through different materials.
They let scientists walk to Earth's center.
questions.modelAnswer: They change behavior as they travel through different materials.

questions.question: What could missing wave patterns suggest about materials inside Earth?
questions.modelAnswer: They could suggest that some waves did not pass through a liquid layer, supporting evidence for a liquid region such as the outer core.

questions.question: Why is seismic evidence described as indirect evidence?
questions.modelAnswer: It is indirect because scientists infer conditions inside Earth from wave behavior instead of directly observing the deep interior.

questions.question: Why should scientists combine seismic evidence with other evidence?
questions.modelAnswer: Combining evidence makes explanations stronger because different kinds of data can support, challenge, or refine the same model.

data.sourcePassage: A mineral is a naturally occurring, nonliving solid with a definite chemical composition and a crystal structure. Minerals can be identified by testing their properties, but color alone is often unreliable. The same mineral may appear in different colors, and different minerals may share a similar color. Scientists use tests such as hardness, streak, luster, cleavage, fracture, density, magnetism, and reaction with acid. In a hardness test, a student checks whether a mineral is scratched by known objects or whether the mineral scratches another object. A streak test shows the color of the mineral's powder. An acid test can help identify calcite because calcite fizzes with weak acid. Students should follow teacher safety directions and should never taste unknown minerals.

data.sourcePassage: Rocks are grouped by how they form. Igneous rocks form when molten material cools and solidifies. Magma cooling slowly underground can form rocks with large visible crystals, such as granite. Lava cooling quickly at or near the surface can form rocks with small crystals, such as basalt. Sedimentary rocks often form when sediment is weathered, eroded, deposited, compacted, and cemented. They may show layers, grains, rounded pieces, or fossils. Sandstone, shale, limestone, and conglomerate are examples. Metamorphic rocks form when existing rocks are changed by heat, pressure, or chemically active fluids without fully melting. Slate can form from shale, marble can form from limestone, and gneiss can form from granite or other rocks. Formation, not just appearance, is the main way scientists classify rocks.

questions.question: Which rock type forms when molten material cools and solidifies?
questions.modelAnswer: Igneous

questions.question: Name one common clue that a rock may be sedimentary.
questions.modelAnswer: Layers, grains, rounded pieces, or fossils can be clues that a rock is sedimentary.

questions.question: Why can large crystals suggest slow cooling underground?
questions.modelAnswer: Large crystals suggest slow cooling because mineral particles had more time to arrange into crystal structures before the rock solidified.

questions.question: How can limestone become marble?
questions.modelAnswer: Limestone can become marble when heat and pressure change it without fully melting it.

questions.question: Why is formation more important than appearance when classifying rocks?
questions.modelAnswer: Formation explains the processes and energy involved in making the rock, while appearance alone can be misleading.

data.sourceTitle: Matter and Energy in the Rock Cycle
data.targetTitle: Matter and Energy in the Rock Cycle
data.sourcePassage: The rock cycle is a model showing how rocks can change from one type to another. It is not a single perfect circle. A rock may follow many different pathways. Matter moves through the cycle as atoms in minerals are rearranged, transported, buried, heated, melted, cooled, crystallized, compacted, or cemented. Energy drives these changes. Heat from Earth's interior can melt rock and cause metamorphism. Energy from the Sun helps power weather and the water cycle, which can weather and erode rocks at Earth's surface. Gravity pulls sediment downhill, while water, wind, and ice transport sediment. Plate movement can bury rocks, lift mountains, and create volcanic activity. Because these processes interact, the rock cycle is a system.

questions.question: What is the rock cycle?
questions.modelAnswer: The rock cycle is a model showing how rocks can change from one type to another.

questions.question: Which energy source helps drive weathering and erosion at Earth's surface?
options: Only pressure from the inner core
questions.modelAnswer: Energy from the Sun

questions.question: How does heat from Earth's interior affect the rock cycle?
questions.modelAnswer: Heat from Earth's interior can melt rock, cause metamorphism, and help drive plate-related processes.

questions.question: Why is it incorrect to say the rock cycle has only one pathway?
questions.modelAnswer: Rocks can change in many different ways; a rock does not have to pass through every stage in the same order.

questions.question: Explain why the rock cycle is a system.
questions.modelAnswer: The rock cycle is a system because matter and energy move through interacting processes such as melting, cooling, weathering, erosion, compaction, cementation, heat, pressure, and plate movement.
